title: Ox Gores Ox: Split the Live One, Split the Dead
kjv_text: And if one man's ox hurt another's, that he die; then they shall sell the live ox, and divide the money of it; and the dead ox also they shall divide. Or if it be known that the ox hath used to push in time past, and his owner hath not kept him in; he shall surely pay ox for ox; and the dead shall be his own.
summary: When one ox kills another: no-fault case, sell the live ox and split both proceeds and carcass; known-gorer case, the negligent owner pays full replacement and keeps the dead animal.
immediate_context: Closes the chapter with the tort system in miniature: loss-sharing for blameless accident, full liability for negligence.
historical_context: Verbatim parallel in Eshnunna 53 — the closest word-for-word match between biblical and Mesopotamian law, the smoking gun of a shared legal tradition. The split-the-loss rule is genuinely elegant: where no one is at fault, both bear half — comparative negligence, three millennia early.
penalty: No-fault: equal division of live-ox proceeds and carcass. Negligence: full ox-for-ox replacement, salvage to payer.
exceptions: Notice (the known gorer) converts sharing into liability.
cross_references: Exodus 22:5-6 (grazing and fire torts, next chapter)
nt_passages: No direct NT engagement; the fault/no-fault distinction resurfaces in parables of stewardship (Luke 12:48, 'to whom much is given').
usofc_implementation: The No-Fault Division Rule: collisions and mutual-damage cases without provable negligence split net loss equally — the basis of the USofC's auto-insurance system, which abolished fault litigation for ordinary crashes. Attested-hazard vehicles (recalled, cited) revert to full liability. Actuaries call it Eshnunna pricing; the Ministry prefers 'Covenant Comparative Fault.'
constitutional_analogue: No-fault insurance statutes (Michigan model), achieved via Bronze Age precedent instead of the 1970s legislature.
scene_ideas: Two drivers splitting a totaled truck's salvage value at an RA kiosk in eleven minutes, both dimly aware this used to take three years and two lawyers.
An actuary's lecture: 'the oldest continuously operating rule in human law is about oxen, and you drive under it.'
satirical_uses: The single most efficient institution in the USofC descends from the one chapter nobody preaches on.
